slides.title: Recap: Reliable AI‑native architectures
slides.notes: Remind students that the previous lecture introduced layered safety mechanisms — guardrails, sandboxing, and human‑in‑the‑loop checkpoints. Emphasize that without measurable signals those layers cannot be validated in production. Connect the idea of observability to today’s focus on quantitative deployment metrics.

slides.title: Why deployment metrics matter
slides.notes: Explain that AI‑native systems change rapidly — model versions, prompt templates, and data pipelines all shift. Without concrete metrics, teams rely on anecdotal evidence. Metrics turn subjective confidence into objective release criteria and feed automated control loops.

slides.title: SLIs and SLOs defined
slides.notes: Define Service Level Indicator (SLI) as a quantifiable measure such as request latency or error count. Service Level Objective (SLO) is the target value the team commits to. Stress that SLOs must be realistic, measurable, and agreed upon by stakeholders. Use the table to illustrate typical pairs for AI‑model serving and micro‑services.

slides.title: Error budgets and burn rate
slides.notes: Error budget quantifies how much unreliability is tolerable before the SLO is violated. Burn rate expresses how fast that budget is being spent. A burn rate above 1× means the budget will be exhausted before the window ends; 2× or higher is a common alert threshold. This concept underpins automated rollback policies.

slides.title: Scenario 1: Microservice deployment walkthrough
bullets: Roll back if SLO breached or burn rate spikes
slides.notes: Walk through a typical canary release: a small traffic slice receives the new build. Real‑time SLIs (p99 latency, 5xx rate) are compared against SLOs. If the new version breaches an SLO or the short‑window burn rate exceeds the alert threshold, the automation rolls back immediately. Otherwise the rollout proceeds.

slides.title: Scenario 2: AI model serving deployment

figure.caption: Blue‑green model swap with budget guard

slides.notes: In blue‑green deployments the new model runs alongside the current one. Traffic is switched atomically. Metrics such as inference latency (p95), token‑generation errors, and safety‑filter rejections are monitored. If the remaining error budget falls below a safety margin, the system automatically reverts to the green (stable) model.

slides.title: Evaluating supplied project metrics step‑by‑step

figure.caption: Safe metric evaluation snippet

slides.notes: Demonstrate a robust evaluation routine that guards against empty log lists (avoiding division by zero) and validates that the SLO’s permitted error rate is positive before computing a budget ratio. Show how the function returns a clear ‘no observations’ marker instead of crashing. This mirrors the safe‑coding practices required for automated rollback pipelines.

slides.title: Hands‑on: Metric evaluation lab
slides.notes: Students pull the provided multi‑component project, execute the metric collector (which emits SLI JSON per service), then apply the evaluation function from the worked problem. They visualise compliance and error‑budget remaining in a simple dashboard (e.g., Grafana or Matplotlib) and decide whether a simulated new release should be rolled back. Instructor circulates to discuss edge cases.

slides.title: Check: Error budget calculation

quiz.question: A service has an SLO of 99.9% availability over a 30‑day window. After 15 days it has experienced 0.05% downtime. What is the remaining error budget as a fraction of the total budget?
quiz.explanation: Total error budget = 0.1% of 30 days = 0.03 day‑equivalents. Consumed = 0.05% of 15 days = 0.0075 day‑equivalents. Remaining = 0.03 - 0.0075 = 0.0225, which is 75% of the total budget. Option A (0.50) incorrectly assumes linear time scaling without accounting for the SLO percentage.

slides.notes: This question tests the ability to compute error‑budget consumption proportionally. The most tempting wrong answer (0.50) comes from assuming half the time means half the budget, ignoring the SLO’s percentage definition.

slides.title: Check: Burn rate interpretation

quiz.question: If a service’s error budget is being consumed at a burn rate of 2.5×, what does this indicate about the remaining budget?
options: Budget will last the full window
Budget will be exhausted before the window ends
Burn rate is irrelevant to budget
quiz.explanation: A burn rate > 1× means the budget is being spent faster than the window’s duration allows; at 2.5× the budget will run out well before the window closes. Option A is the common misconception that any burn rate below 10× is safe.

slides.notes: Reinforces the operational meaning of burn rate. Students often confuse burn‑rate magnitude with absolute safety; the key is the ratio to 1×.

slides.title: Reliability metric dashboards
bullets: Unified view of SLIs across services
slides.notes: Effective dashboards aggregate per‑service SLIs into a single pane of glass. They display current compliance, remaining error budget, and burn‑rate sparklines. Alerting rules are attached to the same pipeline so that operators see the same numbers that automation uses for rollback decisions.

slides.title: Alerting and automated rollback policies
slides.notes: Two common policy tiers: a fast‑burn alert (e.g., >2×) triggers immediate rollback; a slow‑burn alert (budget below 10%) pauses further releases and notifies on‑call. Both are wired into the CI/CD system so that a failing deployment cannot propagate to downstream services.

slides.title: Common pitfalls in metric evaluation
bullets: Dividing by zero on empty logs
slides.notes: Highlight three frequent bugs: (1) naive division by len(logs) when a service has no traffic yet; (2) including cold‑start requests in latency SLIs, which inflates p99; (3) counting harmless validation errors the same as safety‑filter rejections. The worked problem earlier demonstrates a guard against the first pitfall.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Automated rollback needs safe metric code
slides.notes: Conclude by restating that reliable AI‑native deployment hinges on well‑defined SLIs, realistic SLOs, and error‑budget accounting. Emphasize that the automation only works when the metric code handles edge cases (empty logs, zero‑error SLOs). Remind students that the end‑semester assessment will ask them to evaluate a supplied project using exactly these techniques.
